evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Equipping bare PLA arms of an underactuated tarsal-chain-inspired soft gripper with dedicated interfacing structures significantly improves grasping and transport success across diverse everyday objects.

High-friction polymer interfaces dramatically outperform compliant bubble pads and hairy brush strips across almost all arbitrary macroscopic objects, demonstrating that surface friction dominates compliance in universal macroscopic gripping.

Hairy brush interfaces rely primarily on mechanical interlocking with substrate asperities or open grid geometries rather than surface friction, failing completely on smooth surfaces such as ceramic vases and bicycle helmets.

The effective Young's moduli of insect-inspired gripper interface modules range from 1.58e-4 to 12.65e-4 GPa, matching the softness regime of organic cartilage and allowing passive compliance to surface features under compressive gripping loads.

Applying a friction-enhancing rubber spray to highly compliant bubble pads increases grasping success from 0-80% to 33-100%, indicating that structural compliance requires sufficient interface friction to achieve stable grasping.

Direct geometric scaling of biological hairy attachment structures to macroscopic human-scale grippers without contact splitting, stiffness gradients, or specialized tip geometries severely degrades attachment effectiveness due to unfavorable area-to-mass scaling.

experimental_setup: TriTrap bioinspired underactuated soft gripper testing platform with three arms composed of loosely linked tarsomeres 3D-printed from PLA.

Modular snap-on fixtures fabricated via FDM 3D printing (Prusa Mk3S, 0.4 mm nozzle, 0.2 mm layer thickness) with PLA base, glued to U-shaped packaging foam pieces (Repair Max glue), and fitted with self-adhering Velcro.

Three bioinspired interface strip variants: (1) Dycem non-slip polymer film (friction tape), (2) air-filled polymeric bubble pads (untreated and treated with gloveGlu rubber spray), and (3) compliant synthetic brush strips (2000 hairs/cm^2, 1 cm length, 0.05 mm diameter; untreated and treated with gloveGlu rubber spray).

ZwickRoell Z 0.5 linear tensile/compression testing system equipped with custom fixtures to evaluate compressive force-displacement response and effective Young's moduli under maximum loads of 20, 25, and 30 N.

Custom in-house slanted-slip testing device with a tiltable platform (1 deg/s angular velocity) and support block to evaluate static friction coefficients on planar cork, fabric, glass, and plastic substrates.

Qualitative transport tests (lifting and transporting 1 m) on six baseline objects: electric water boiler (600 g), PC keyboard (400 g), textile bag (40 g), polystyrene vase (20 g), plastic bottle (30 g), and steel grill attachment (160 g).

Quantitative grasping tests (30 attempts per object in two random orientations, requiring a lift and 3 s hover) on six new objects: cardboard profile (140 g), kitchen paper package (750 g), plastic canister (515 g), ceramic vase (1500 g), bicycle helmet (400 g), and filament spool (285 g).
future_work: Developing compound/hybrid interface modules combining distinct specialized structures (e.g., friction pads, soft compliant bubbles, and interlocking setae/claws) to exploit multi-scale synergistic effects on heterogeneous roughnesses.
Further investigation and optimization of patterned, pad-like microstructures on soft gripping surfaces.
Case-specific testing and evaluation for concrete application environments in agriculture, industry, medicine, housekeeping, and space exploration.
Varying hair dimensions (e.g., evaluating shorter, stiffer hairs for shear resistance on asperities versus longer hairs for macroscopic feature conformability).
Incorporating biological principles such as contact splitting, hierarchical structuring, stiffness gradients, and shaped tip geometries into synthetic hairy interface designs.

surface friction treatment state of bubble and brush modules (untreated vs. treated with gloveGlu rubber spray)
substrate material in friction testing (cork, glass, fabric, plastic)
test object properties (geometry, weight, surface morphology, material, and 2 random orientations across 12 distinct objects)
maximum compressive load in mechanical indentation testing (20 N, 25 N, 30 N)
limitations_inferred: Manual actuation by a human operator introduces operator-dependent variability in pulling velocity, peak tendon force, and arm closing trajectories.
Static friction characterization was conducted exclusively on flat, rigid substrates, which may not capture friction dynamics on curved, compliant, or irregular geometries.
Dynamic friction, wear endurance, shear fatigue, and adhesive degradation over extended cyclic grasping were not assessed.
Testing only two arbitrary orientations per object may not encompass edge-case grasping poses encountered in automated manipulation.
The use of repurposed packaging foam and Velcro introduces uncontrolled compliance, damping, and potential interfacial hysteresis between the gripper structure and the contact pad.
limitations_stated_by_authors: The study is exploratory in nature, establishing qualitative guidelines rather than definitive conclusions for specific use-cases.
Actuation was executed manually via a handle pulled by a human operator without direct measurement of the applied input actuation force.
The TriTrap gripper platform adopted an underactuated single-tendon channel and did not replicate the multiple passive degrees of freedom present in natural insect tarsal chains.
Gripper interfacing principles were unoptimized beyond their basic conceptual differentiation.
The brush hairs were composed of an unknown polymer and had flat cut-off tips rather than the specialized tip geometries found on insect adhesive setae.
Natural stiffness gradients along the length of hairs or surrounding cuticle were not replicated in the artificial brush strips.
Scaling constraints (surface area scaling with length squared while mass scales with length cubed) impede the effectiveness of macroscopic hair arrays without contact splitting.
Original bubble and brush materials had very low baseline surface friction, necessitating post-hoc rubber spray treatment to decouple compliance from friction.
main_results: Effective compressive Young's moduli of all modules were within 1.58e-4 to 12.65e-4 GPa (comparable to organic cartilage); brushes showed three distinct stiffness regimes (regime II: 1.58e-4 GPa, regime III: 6.53e-4 GPa), bubbles showed 6.76e-4 GPa, and friction tape showed 12.65e-4 GPa along with a 0.82 N pull-off adhesion effect.

Friction tape yielded the highest static friction coefficients on plastic (28.63) and glass (9.51), whereas brushes achieved higher friction on rough substrates via interlocking (cork: 2.05, fabric: 1.60); bubble pads exhibited low static friction (~0.62 to 0.67) across all substrates.
In qualitative baseline tests, equipped interface modules succeeded on the first attempt across all objects except the water boiler using bubbles or brushes (which failed, mirroring bare arms).
In quantitative tests, friction tape was superior across all objects (96.6% to 100% success rate), including the 1500 g ceramic vase and bicycle helmet.

Untreated bubble pads achieved 0% success on the vase and helmet and 10% to 80% on other objects, but rubber spray treatment increased success to 100% on paper, cardboard, and vase, 93% on spool, 63% on canister, and 33% on helmet.

Untreated brushes succeeded at 100% on cardboard and the honeycomb filament spool due to mechanical interlocking, but scored 0% on the smooth vase and helmet; rubber spray had only minor effects on brush success (increasing paper package success from 6.7% to 30.0% and canister from 23.3% to 26.7%).
Chi-square statistical tests confirmed significant differences in gripping success between interfacing modules for all tested objects (p < 0.001).

calculation of static coefficient of friction from slip onset angles on a slanted-slip platform
chi-square statistical significance testing using Sigmaplot 12.0

gripping success rate (percentage of successful lifts and 3 s hovers out of 30 trials)

possible_gap_implications: Demonstrating that interface friction dominates structural compliance in macroscopic grasping challenges the design paradigm that soft robotic conformability alone ensures stable grasping, pointing toward friction-enhanced skin engineering as a primary research gap.

The failure of macroscopic synthetic hair arrays on smooth surfaces reveals that direct geometric scale-up of bioinspired setae is insufficient without implementing hierarchical contact splitting and local stiffness gradients.

The complementary performance of interlocking brushes on perforated/fibrous objects versus friction tape on smooth surfaces suggests a need for spatially heterogeneous or multi-material hybrid contact surfaces on soft robot fingers.
paper.research_objective: To establish a qualitative guideline for estimating the performance-enhancing effects of three insect-inspired interfacing mechanisms (friction tape, compliant soft bubble pads, and interlocking hairy brush strips) on soft robotic gripping across diverse macroscopic objects and surface morphologies using the bioinspired TriTrap gripper platform.
paper.research_problem: Soft robotic grippers excel at compliance and contact area formation, but bare, hard gripper arms often fail to establish secure contact along their lengths and default to tip clamping; furthermore, the specific roles and comparative efficacy of biological contact enhancement principles (high friction, structural compliance, and fibrillar interlocking) remain insufficiently characterized and often neglected in soft gripper design.
paper.robot_type: soft robotic gripper (biomimetic underactuated tarsal-chain TriTrap gripper)
stiffness_mechanism: loosely linked tarsomere chain with elastic joint relaxation
Young's modulus gradient from contact interface to bulk structural backing
paper.title: Comparison of interfacing mechanics for soft robotic grippers
